text: On the day shift at Rig 4, a company employee was operating the hydraulic winch when the guard rail on the boom collapsed. The employee was only a few feet away from the moving arm, but the guard held it in place until a last‑minute manual check restored the barrier. The incident was a close call that could have resulted in serious injury if the guard had not been re‑installed.

Night shift in Pipeline Yard D: a company employee started to climb the manhole ladder to enter a storage tank for a routine inspection, but the ladder was slanted and slipped on the wet concrete. He grabbed the ladder rung to steady himself and almost fell into the tank. The tank cover was not in place, so the employee had to quickly exit and call for a safety barrier to be erected before any real damage could happen.

On the night shift at Rig 4, a contractor was walking across the open trench area without his hard hat and safety vest. He was wearing a loose jacket and had his safety goggles on, but his head and torso were not protected. I stopped him and explained that the trench was a fall hazard and he needed full PPE before proceeding.

During the night shift at Terminal C, a contractor was walking toward the storage dock when his shoe slipped on a slick patch of oil that had spilled from a damaged pipe. He almost slipped and nearly twisted his ankle, but the ground was still firm enough that he managed to regain balance without falling. The spill was immediately cleaned up and a warning sign was placed in the area.

During the night shift at Storage Site E, a company employee was walking along the loading dock when a forklift driver, distracted by a radio, failed to notice the pedestrian and nearly collided. The operator had to brake hard and the employee was only slightly shaken, but a safety barrier that should have been installed along the aisle was missing, which allowed the vehicle to enter the pedestrian zone. Thankfully, no one was seriously hurt, but the incident highlighted a clear gap in the site’s traffic control.

On the night shift at Rig 4, a company employee was walking down the access corridor without wearing a hard hat. The employee slipped on a loose pipe and nearly fell onto the hot piping, but the fall was stopped by a nearby safety barrier. The incident highlighted that the worker was not wearing the required PPE and the lack of a hard hat increased the risk of head injury.

At Rig 4 during the day shift, a company employee entered the sump pit to replace a sensor. He forgot to secure the ladder with a fall‑protection line and slipped on a wet edge, nearly falling into the pit. Thankfully, the floor’s metal guardrail held him back, but the incident shows a clear lapse in the confined space entry procedure.

Night shift in Pipeline Yard D, a contractor was inspecting a new pipe joint when he noticed a faint odor of gas. He stopped work, checked the pressure gauge and found the pressure slightly high but no visible leak; he called the supervisor and had the area isolated with a temporary fire extinguisher. The contractor kept a safe distance while the leak source was identified and sealed, preventing any fire.

During the day shift at Terminal C, a contractor was walking across the storage area when a pile of pallets had been left in front of the loading dock. He slipped on the wet surface and nearly fell onto the forklift tracks. The contractor was able to recover before any collision, but the incident showed the spill containment strip had been removed for maintenance and not replaced.

During the day shift at Pipeline Yard D, a contractor was working on the support tower when a temporary guardrail that had been removed for a quick inspection slipped and collapsed. The contractor fell about four feet onto the metal rail below, breaking his wrist but managing to grab the rail to stop a larger injury. The fall was a near miss that highlighted the need to secure the guardrail before lifting the tools.

During the night shift at Maintenance Shop H, I was walking the perimeter when a delivery truck backed out of the loading bay too quickly. The driver didn’t see me and almost ran over my feet; I had to jump aside at the last second. Luckily no one was hit and I only got a slight bruise, but the incident shows our pedestrian‑vehicle safety protocols need tightening.

During the day shift at Pipeline Yard D, a company employee was walking across the loading dock when a delivery truck backed up too close to the pedestrian path. The driver was distracted by a radio, and the employee had to step aside at the last second. No one was injured, but the truck’s stopping distance was longer than usual, and the employee noted the lack of a clear barrier or signage to keep pedestrians out of the vehicle zone.

At Terminal C on the night shift, a contractor was walking through the loading bay when he didn’t wear his safety gloves or helmet. He slipped on a wet patch and nearly fell into a pool of diesel that was leaking from a damaged pipe. Luckily, the spill was contained and no one was injured, but the incident shows how critical PPE compliance is, especially in a high‑risk area like that.

During the night shift at Rig 4, a contractor was operating a hydraulic winch when the safety lockout tag was missing from the control panel. The winch slipped and the load swung toward the rig platform, narrowly missing the crew. The incident showed a clear equipment machinery hazard due to the absent safety barrier.

At Rig 4 during the day shift, a company employee was preparing to enter the wellhead enclosure for maintenance. While setting up the isolation valve, the employee noticed the gas detector reading was elevated, but the safety barrier was still in place. The employee decided to wait for a safety officer to confirm the area was safe before proceeding, avoiding a potential confined space entry hazard.

While on the day shift at Pipeline Yard D, a company employee was walking across the intersection when a delivery truck coming in from the loading bay ran a red light and swerved into the pedestrian crossing. The driver didn't see the pedestrian because the guardrail that normally separates vehicles from the crossing was missing, leaving the employee only a few feet from being hit. The employee stepped back just in time, but the truck's bumper clipped his shoulder and the guardrail broke. The incident was logged as a near miss, and the yard manager is ordering immediate replacement of the missing barrier.

Night shift at Refinery B: A contractor was walking across the loading dock when a maintenance vehicle, driven by an on‑site employee, accelerated too quickly and almost clipped him. The contractor narrowly avoided being hit, but the incident shows the need for better traffic control signage in that area. No one was injured, but the near‑miss highlighted how easily the crew could get caught in vehicle traffic.

At Terminal C on the night shift, a contractor was working on the roof of the storage silos. While setting up a ladder, he stepped off the top rung and fell about three feet to the concrete floor, scraping his knee. The fall was a near‑miss that could have been worse if the ladder had not been properly secured.

During the day shift on Rig 4, I saw a company employee walking through the welding zone without wearing the required safety glasses or hearing protection. The employee was standing very close to an active hot‑work area, and a spark from a nearby torch almost hit their face before the operator realized the breach and backed away. The incident highlighted a clear lapse in PPE compliance that could have led to serious eye or ear injury.

During the night shift at Refinery B, a contractor was working on the valve pit without a face shield, despite the visible PPE signage. The contractor’s visor slipped off, and he almost hit the hot pipe that was still in operation, but the safety gate kept him from serious injury. The incident shows the contractor ignored PPE requirements, creating a near‑miss situation.

During the day shift at Refinery B, a contractor was walking across the maintenance corridor when he slipped on a patch of oil that had leaked from a nearby pipe. The spill had not been marked with a warning tape, and there was no spill containment barrier in place, so the contractor stumbled but managed to catch himself on a handrail before falling. The incident highlighted a slip‑trip hazard due to the missing spill containment barrier and unmarked oil spill.

Late night on Rig 4, a company employee was walking toward the loading dock when a maintenance truck backed out of the bay and almost ran into him. The driver missed the employee’s position by only a couple of feet, and the truck’s rear camera didn’t display the obstacle. Luckily, the employee stepped back just in time and no one was injured, but the incident highlights how the pedestrian walkway was too close to the vehicle turnaround path.

During the night shift at Refinery B, I saw a company employee walking in the high‑pressure line area without the required hard hat and safety boots. He was just about to walk past a flashing hazard sign when the protective barrier on the railing fell apart, and he almost lost his balance. Luckily, the guard rail was still intact enough to stop him, but the incident shows how bad PPE noncompliance can lead to near‑misses.

Night shift at Rig 4: a contractor was attempting to enter the maintenance hatch of the storage tank. He didn’t secure the proper lock‑out tag and the hatch remained open. While he was inside, the ventilation fan tripped off, and he could feel the air getting stale. Luckily he got out before any gas build‑up happened, but the hatch lock was still missing.

During the day shift at Refinery B, a company employee was working on the 500 bar line when the isolation valve failed to lock. The valve slipped open while the worker was disconnecting the feed pipe, causing a sudden surge of hot fluid. Luckily the safety interlock on the control panel tripped, and the worker was able to jump out of the way before the fluid hit the equipment. The incident was reported and the valve is now being replaced.

During the day shift at Refinery B, a contractor was working on a maintenance task near the pressure vessel when the lockout tag was accidentally removed. The vessel was still pressurized, so a sudden pressure release sent a burst of steam toward the worker’s face, forcing him to step back. Fortunately, the contractor only suffered a minor burn and was able to get medical attention on site.

At Pipeline Yard D during the night shift, a company employee was walking through the yard with his hard hat off and no gloves on while moving a stack of pipe fittings. He slipped on a wet patch near the storage bin and the fitting he was handling slid off his hands, rolling toward the rail line. The falling pipe could have hit the train tracks, but a safety guard was in place that stopped it from reaching the rails. The employee was shaken but only suffered a minor bruised elbow.

While moving a tanker across the loading area in Pipeline Yard D during the day shift, an employee slipped on a wet patch near the top of the stack and lost balance. He fell about 2 feet to the concrete floor but landed on a padded guardrail that was just installed, so he only sustained a minor bruise. The incident highlighted that the slip‑resistant coating on that section was still drying.

At Loading Bay G during the day shift, a contractor was unloading a gas tanker when the valve on the tank’s gas line popped off, releasing a small burst of vapour. The vapour drifted toward the storage area and sparked a weak flame that quickly fizzled out, but the contractor had to move back a few metres before the flare could spread. Luckily the safety barrier around the tanker was missing, so the spill could have gotten worse, but we managed to contain it with the portable fire extinguisher on site.

During the night shift at Drilling Unit F, a company employee slipped on a wet patch near the feed line. The spill had come from a leaking hose that wasn’t marked, so the worker stumbled and almost fell onto the heavy equipment, but a quick reaction kept him from serious injury. The incident highlights the missing spill containment that created a slip‑trip hazard.

At Rig 4 on the night shift, a company employee was walking along the perimeter when a service truck backed out of a loading bay and clipped a barrier that had been removed for maintenance. The employee was pushed but didn’t get hurt; the barrier should have stopped the truck. It was a close call that exposed the need to keep all safety rails in place, even during routine work.

During the night shift at Refinery B, a contractor was tightening a valve on the gas line when a sudden pressure spike caused a small section of the pipe to crack. The contractor heard a hiss and saw a faint blue gas plume, but the flame arrestor had been removed for maintenance, so the gas didn’t ignite. The contractor quickly shut the line off and sealed the crack with a patch kit before the gas could spread.

During the day shift at Drilling Unit F, a company employee noticed a faint burning smell coming from the gas line near the rig floor. He stopped the line and checked the pressure gauge, but the gas flow had already spurted slightly onto the exposed pipe, creating a small flame that was quickly smothered with a fire blanket. The employee reported the incident, and we shut down the unit for a full inspection of the gas leak system.

During the day shift at Terminal C, a company employee slipped on a wet patch while walking near the top of the loading dock and lost his footing, falling about two feet down onto the concrete floor. He was shaken but only sustained a minor bruise, and the incident highlighted that the anti-slip mats in that area need replacement.

During the night shift at Refinery B, a company employee slipped on a wet patch near the valve pit while moving a tank. The spill had been cleaned but no warning tape was laid out, so the worker almost fell into the pit and only caught themselves on a nearby pipe. The slip caused a minor injury to the wrist and highlighted a missing slip‑trip barrier.

During the day shift on Rig 4, a company employee began entering a maintenance hatch that was not properly sealed. He noticed a faint odor of diesel fumes but was not wearing a full respirator because the rack was missing. The hatch latch slipped and he slipped slightly, catching his glove, but he was able to pull himself out before any serious injury occurred. The incident shows the hatch’s safety barrier was not in place, posing a real confined space risk.

During the night shift at Drilling Unit F, a company employee slipped on a wet patch near the top of the scaffold and fell about two feet before he hit the padded floor. He only sustained a bruised arm, but the incident showed that the safety railing was not properly positioned, so the guardrail system failed to prevent the slip. The crew immediately secured the area, replaced the broken railing, and reminded everyone to keep the walkways dry.

At Rig 4 during the night shift, a contractor slipped on a slick patch of oil near the hoist station because the spill cover had been removed for maintenance and the spill containment tray was not in place. He caught himself on the rig ladder, but the ladder was already damp and he almost lost his footing. The spill area was marked with a red flag, but the flag was too close to the edge, so the contractor walked into the hazard zone without noticing it.

During the day shift at Terminal C, a company employee noticed a faint orange glow from the storage tank area, indicating a possible gas leak. He immediately stopped work, shouted a warning, and walked to the fire alarm system, which rang promptly. The employee was able to evacuate the zone before any flame appeared, and the gas detector later confirmed a small leak that was quickly sealed by the maintenance crew.

While clearing the storage area at Terminal C on the day shift, a contractor was passing a gas cylinder through the loading dock. The cylinder’s valve was not fully closed, and a small hiss of gas escaped, but the contractor quickly noticed the odor and stopped, sealing the valve immediately. No flames or ignition source was present, and no one was exposed to any dangerous concentration of gas. The contractor’s quick reaction prevented a potential fire or explosion near the terminal.

During the night shift at Storage Site E, a contractor was lowering a pallet of piping from a 4‑meter high scaffold. The safety bar that should have been in place to prevent falling was missing, so the pallet slipped off the edge and hit the concrete floor below, but the contractor was not injured. He realized the bar had been removed for a previous repair and that no temporary guardrail had been installed.

During the night shift at Refinery B, a contractor was repairing a roof vent when the guard rail he was standing on collapsed. He fell only a few feet onto the concrete floor and got a minor cut on his hand, but the fall almost hit the adjacent piping. Thankfully no one else was hurt.

During the day shift at Drilling Unit F, a company employee was observed walking through the high‑pressure pipe corridor without wearing the required hard hat and safety glasses. The employee’s lack of PPE left him vulnerable to potential falling debris, but fortunately no equipment fell during that moment. The incident was logged as a near‑miss, and the crew was reminded to check PPE compliance before re‑entering the area.

During the day shift at Storage Site E, a company employee tripped over a loose cable that had fallen from a higher level pipe. The employee caught himself on a nearby stack of barrels and was able to continue work with only a minor back strain, but the incident revealed that the cable was not properly secured and the area lacked a clear warning sign. The employee reported the tripping hazard to the supervisor, and the cable was immediately re‑wrapped and the spot marked with a caution tape.

During the night shift on Rig 4 a contractor was working on the top of the platform when he lost his footing on a wet edge. He slipped and fell about three feet before the guardrail caught his foot, breaking his wrist. The fall was prevented from being more serious because the safety barrier was intact and the fall arrest system was engaged.

During the night shift at Storage Site E, a contractor was working on the roof of the storage tank when he slipped off the edge of the platform. He caught himself on a nearby pipe but twisted his ankle and had to be moved to the on‑site medical bay. The fall risk was high because the guardrail had been removed for maintenance and no temporary barrier was in place.

During the day shift at Refinery B, a company employee slipped on a patch of oil that had leaked from a cracked pipe near the conveyor line. The floor was slick and there was no spill containment barrier in place, so the worker stumbled but caught himself on the nearby rail. He didn't fall, but the incident highlighted that a spill containment system was missing and should be installed immediately.

During the day shift at Storage Site E, a contractor was performing routine valve checks when he attempted to lockout the main feed line. The lockout tag was missing, and the valve remained energized; the contractor was forced to shut the line manually, but the line spurted out a burst of steam that knocked him off balance. He was able to get up without injury, but the incident exposed a clear energy isolation failure.

At Pipeline Yard D on the day shift, a company employee was attempting to enter a sealed steel trough for maintenance. The lockout tag on the entry hatch was not properly engaged, so the employee slipped and the hatch popped open, dropping a piece of steel into the trough. The employee narrowly avoided a serious injury by grabbing the hatch in time, but the incident shows a clear failure of the safety barrier.

Night shift at Rig 4, a contractor was entering a pump room without the required breathing hood. He slipped on a wet patch, nearly fell into the sump, and only stopped when the safety guard was pulled down manually. The incident highlighted that the confined‑space entry barrier was missing and the contractor had not checked for the presence of a proper ventilation system before starting work.

While unloading a delivery truck at Terminal C during the night shift, a contractor tripped over a loose pallet that had been left on the concrete deck. The contractor fell forward but managed to grab the railing and avoided a serious injury. The pallet was not marked as a hazard and the area was not flagged for caution, creating a slip/trip risk for anyone working nearby.

During the night shift on Rig 4, a company employee walking across the main access lane was almost hit by a service truck that didn't notice the pedestrian until the last second. The driver saw the employee just in time and stopped, but the employee had to step back and was shaken. The incident highlighted that the temporary speed‑limit sign had been misplaced, so it didn’t warn the driver about the pedestrian crossing.

During the day shift at Drilling Unit F, a company employee was walking across the access lane when a maintenance truck, stopped in the middle of the lane, failed to stop in time. The truck’s driver was distracted by a radio conversation and didn’t see the employee until the worker was just inches away, causing a collision that knocked the employee off his feet and she sprained her ankle. The incident was a near‑miss for serious injury, but the lack of a safety barrier in that lane let the driver’s path cross the pedestrian route.

During the night shift in Pipeline Yard D, a company employee was working on valve 12 when the energy isolation lock failed to engage. He heard a sudden hiss of gas as the valve opened automatically, and the pressure surge blew the protective cover off. Thankfully, the employee stepped back just in time, but the burst cover scattered shrapnel across the yard, causing a small cut on his forearm.

During the day shift at Rig 4, a company employee noticed a faint odor of gas near the drilling rig. The employee shut down the valve but the pressure relief vent was not properly sealed, so a small flame briefly flickered on the surface of the rig’s piping. Thankfully, the fire suppression system activated immediately and the flame was contained before it could spread. The employee reported the near miss and the missing safety barrier to the shift supervisor.

At Pipeline Yard D during the day shift a contractor was walking back from the loading bay and slipped on a patch of wet oil that had seeped onto the concrete floor. The contractor immediately caught himself on a nearby pallet and avoided a fall, but the slick spot was a clear slip‑trip hazard that could have caused a serious injury. The spill was cleaned up quickly after the incident and a warning sign was posted until the area was dry.

Night shift at Rig 4: a contractor was working on the downhole valve when the isolation lock failed to engage; he slipped, the valve opened suddenly, and a spray of hot fluid hit the ground just a few feet away. He only got a minor burn and no one else was harmed, but the barrier that should have kept the hot fluid from escaping was missing.

Night shift at Pipeline Yard D, a company employee was walking toward the loading dock when a maintenance truck started moving without a stop sign in place. The driver didn’t see the pedestrian until the truck was almost at the person, and the employee had to jump out of the way at the last moment. The truck’s horn didn’t sound, and the safety barrier that normally separates the pedestrian path from the vehicle lane was missing, making the incident close to a collision.

At Rig 4 during the day shift a contractor was working on the gas line when the isolation valve failed to lock. He tried to shut it off, but the valve slipped and gas started leaking into the control room. The contractor had to pull back and the crew had to shut down the operation to ventilate the area.

During the day shift at Terminal C, a company employee was attempting to perform routine maintenance on the storage tank manifold when the energy isolation switch failed to lock. The valve was still live and the employee slipped, nearly contacting the high-pressure pipe. Luckily the safety guard rail was still in place, stopping a serious injury.

Night shift at Terminal C: an employee was climbing the maintenance ladder to replace a light fixture. He slipped on a wet rung and fell about 3 feet onto the concrete floor. Luckily, he only got a minor bruise and the fall was stopped by the guard rail that was already in place, but the ladder was damaged and needs replacement.

While performing the night shift maintenance at Storage Site E, I noticed a faint orange glow coming from the tank roof area. The employee was working under the tank when a small burst of gas slipped through a cracked pipe, but the fire alarm system kicked in instantly and the crew pulled the emergency shut‑off. No one was hurt, but the cracked pipe needs to be replaced before the next shift.

During the day shift at Refinery B, a company employee slipped on a wet patch left by a leaking pipe in the maintenance bay. The floor had a small, unmarked spill that wasn't cleared, so the worker lost balance and almost dropped his toolbox. Luckily he caught himself on the nearby wall, but the incident highlighted that the spill had not been properly flagged or cleaned.

During the day shift at Terminal C, a contractor was attempting to work on the pressure line when the isolation valve failed to close properly. The valve remained partially open, letting a small burst of high-pressure gas escape, but the safety barrier had been removed for maintenance, so no one was directly hit. The contractor quickly shut the valve manually and sealed the line, but the incident highlighted that the isolation system was not reliable and could have caused a serious release if the valve had not been manually overridden.

During the day shift at Drilling Unit F, a contractor was moving a hydraulic line when the energy isolation valve for the drilling rig failed to close. The line started to discharge fluid under pressure, and the contractor had to quickly shut off the supply with a backup valve. Luckily, no one was injured, but the incident shows the isolation system wasn’t reliable and could have caused a serious spill if a safety barrier had been missing.

During the night shift at Pipeline Yard D, a company employee was climbing a 12‑foot maintenance ladder to replace a valve on a storage tank when the ladder slipped from its footing. The employee fell a few inches but landed on a padded mat, suffering only a bruised wrist. The fall highlighted that the ladder’s stabilizer was missing and the area lacked a proper guardrail.

Night shift at Refinery B: a contractor was welding on a pipe line that had been left in the “on‑line” state because the energy isolation lockout was not properly engaged. When the valve opened, hot steam burst out, splashing the contractor and forcing him to jump back. Thankfully he was only splashed and didn’t sustain any serious injury, but the incident shows the isolation failure risk.

During the day shift on Rig 4 a contractor was moving a pallet of spare parts along the gangway. The floor was slick with a spill of hydraulic fluid that had not been cleaned up, and the contractor slipped, almost falling into the open wellhead shaft. The safety barrier around the wellhead was missing that day, so the slip could have led to a serious fall.

During the night shift at Refinery B, a contractor was working on the roof of the storage tank when his safety harness slipped from its anchor point. He fell a few feet onto the concrete floor, but was caught by a nearby guardrail before any serious injury. The incident highlighted that the harness lanyard was old and had not been inspected, and the guardrail was not properly secured.

Night shift at Rig 4, a contractor was welding a pipe bracket when the safety guard on the hydraulic jack slipped off. He nearly dropped the jack onto the ground, but it just bounced back, and nobody was hurt. The guard should have been secured or replaced before the job.

At Refinery B on the day shift, a company employee was working on the maintenance of the centrifugal separator when the guard on the motor housing came loose and the wheel spun out, nearly catching his forearm. The safety barrier around the motor was missing, so the employee had to step in quickly to pull the wheel back into place. The incident was a close call, but no one was hurt.

At the loading bay G during the night shift, a company employee was working on the tank line when the valve isolation lock slipped, leaving the line still energized. He noticed a small spark when he tried to pull the valve open, and immediately shut down the feed line to stop the flow. The incident was a near‑miss; the equipment didn’t rupture, but the failure of the isolation lock posed a serious risk of a high‑pressure release.

On the day shift at Terminal C, a company employee slipped on a wet patch left after a routine spill clean‑up. The employee nearly fell over a short gap between the walkway and a storage rack, but the guardrail prevented a fall. The spill was not covered in time and the gap was not marked, creating a slip‑trip hazard.

During the day shift at Refinery B, a company employee was walking through the piping corridor without a hard hat or safety glasses, ignoring the posted PPE signs. As a heavy pipe crane passed overhead, the employee's head was almost struck by a hanging pipe, narrowly avoiding injury. The incident highlights a clear PPE noncompliance that could have caused serious harm.

During the night shift at Terminal C, a company employee was operating a conveyor belt that feeds raw material into the storage tanks. While performing a routine inspection, the employee noticed the safety guard on the belt had been removed to facilitate cleaning and was not replaced. The belt slipped, and the employee was almost caught by the moving belt. The guard was not in place, creating a clear equipment machinery hazard.

During the day shift at Rig 4, a company employee slipped on a wet patch near the loading chute because the spill marker had been removed and the area wasn’t flagged. The employee caught themselves and avoided injury, but the spill still posed a trip risk for anyone in the zone. The crew noted that the barrier pad was missing and the spill containment plan was not updated.

During the night shift at Pipeline Yard D, a company employee was checking a valve when a sudden hiss of gas was heard. The gas escaped from a cracked line right beside the worker, but the fire suppression system kicked in quickly and the gas dispersed before it could ignite. The employee managed to escape safely, and the incident was logged as a near‑miss.

At Loading Bay G during the day shift, a contractor was seen walking through the hazardous spill area without a face mask or safety boots. He was only wearing a jacket and gloves, so he risked inhaling vapors and getting cut by exposed piping. The supervisor noticed immediately and called him to stop, but the contractor kept moving because he thought the hazard was minor. The incident was recorded as a near‑miss since no injury occurred but the PPE violation could have caused serious harm.

During the night shift at Refinery B, a company employee slipped on a wet patch near the storage tank that had not been flagged with a warning sign. He caught himself on the edge of a maintenance ladder but lost balance, almost falling onto the piping below. The spill had come from a leaking valve that was not cleaned up after the day shift, creating a clear slip risk that went unnoticed. The employee was fine but the incident highlighted that the spill area lacked proper signage and barriers.

During the day shift on Rig 4, a contractor was tightening a gas line when a loose fitting popped off, releasing a burst of gas that quickly ignited a small flame at the pipe junction. The contractor was only a few feet away but managed to move out of the way before the fire spread; the incident was contained with the portable extinguisher on standby. The fire alarm sounded, and the crew evacuated the area, but no one was injured.

On the day shift at Terminal C, I saw a company employee walking near the loading bay without a hard hat or safety glasses. He was reaching for a pallet of chemicals and almost got his hand caught in a moving conveyor belt, but he stopped just in time. The incident was a close call and showed that the employee was not following the required PPE policy.

While walking from the mud pit to the rig bay on the night shift at Rig 4, I saw a company employee standing beside the 50‑bar riser pipe without a harness or safety lanyard. He was holding a large drill bit in one hand and a steel jackhammer in the other, and he was ignoring the posted safety signage that required a full body harness in that area. The employee slipped on a slick patch of mud, lost his balance, and the jackhammer swung, narrowly missing his own head and a nearby support beam. The fall was stopped by the rig’s overhead safety barrier, but the incident exposed a clear lapse in PPE compliance that could have caused serious injury if the employee had hit the pipe or fallen into the wellhead.

Night shift on Rig 4, a contractor was seen walking across the open trench area without wearing the required safety harness and hard‑hat. He slipped on a patch of loose gravel and nearly fell into the excavation; a safety guard had been removed for maintenance and was not in place. The incident was flagged immediately and the contractor was sent back to the yard to re‑equip with proper PPE before re‑entering the work zone.

During the night shift at Terminal C, a company employee was standing beside the loading conveyor when the safety guard on the machine had fallen off and was not in place. The guard was supposed to prevent the worker from getting caught in the moving parts, but it was missing, so the employee almost got his hand snagged. He stopped the conveyor and reported the missing guard to the supervisor.

During the night shift on Rig 4, a contractor was walking across the concrete pad without wearing the required hard hat and safety glasses. The contractor clipped his sleeve against the edge of a support beam, nearly falling onto the hot pipe that was still in operation. The incident was reported as a near miss, but the lack of PPE was noted as a serious noncompliance issue.

During the night shift at Terminal C, a company employee entered a storage tank without using the required pressure gauge check. He stopped to check the valve handle but the tank pressure rose to a hazardous level while he was inside. Luckily the emergency shut‑off was activated before any serious exposure occurred, but the incident shows the confined space entry protocol was not followed.

At Terminal C on the day shift, a company employee entered a maintenance hatch on the fuel storage tank without first checking the pressure gauge; the hatch was not marked as a confined space entry point and no air quality test had been done. As the worker descended, a burst of stale air escaped, causing him to cough and stumble. He pulled himself back to the platform, and the supervisor immediately shut off the ventilation fan and called for a confined space rescue team.

Night shift at Terminal C, a company employee slipped on a wet patch near the storage rack and nearly fell onto the pipeline. He quickly braced himself, but the slick surface was due to a leaking hose that hadn't been marked. The spill was cleaned up after the incident, and a temporary spill marker was placed.

During the day shift in Maintenance Shop H, a company employee was working on the hydraulic pump assembly. While preparing to start the motor, he found that the lockout tag on the power switch was missing, and the isolation valve was not fully closed. The employee realized that the energy isolation had failed, so he immediately shut the motor down and called the supervisor, but a burst of hydraulic fluid sprayed onto his boots, causing a minor burn.

During the night shift at Rig 4, a company employee was working on the blow‑out preventer set‑up when the isolation valve failed to close properly. The valve stayed open, and a small burst of pressure pushed a section of the pipe outward, but the employee stopped it in time and quickly shut the main safety valve, preventing a major release. The incident highlights the risk of energy isolation failures on the rig.

During the day shift at Refinery B, a company employee was working on the crude distillation unit when the energy isolation valve failed to lock. The valve stayed open, allowing high pressure steam to surge through the pipe and nearly caused a rupture. Fortunately, the employee was wearing a safety barrier and stopped the flow with a manual shutoff, but the incident shows the isolation system was not functioning properly.

Night shift at Drilling Unit F, a company employee slipped on the wet edge of the hatch and fell onto the concrete floor. The fall was just enough to scrape his knees, but it exposed a gap in the guardrail that was supposed to be there. He was able to get up and call for a quick cleanup; no one else was in the area at the time.

During the day shift at Rig 4, a contractor was seen walking around the drilling pit without a hard hat and the required high-visibility vest. He was approaching the hydraulic pump area where a safety barrier had been removed for maintenance, and he nearly slipped on the loose bit of equipment that had fallen from the platform. The missing barrier and lack of PPE meant he could have been hit by the moving pump arm, but the crew stopped him in time.

During the day shift on Rig 4, a contractor was working on the rig floor when a step ladder he had set up collapsed because the locking mechanism had not been engaged. He fell about a meter down but landed on a nearby padded mat, breaking his arm. The incident was recorded as a near‑miss because the fall was caught by the guardrail that was properly installed.

Night shift at Refinery B: a company employee was working on the crude distillation column. He forgot to lock out the control valve before performing a maintenance check, and the valve opened when the column was depressurized, releasing a surge of hot vapor that nearly sprayed him. The energy isolation failed and he was able to avoid injury, but the incident showed a serious lapse in lock‑out/tag‑out procedure.

At Loading Bay G on the night shift, a company employee was walking across the loading dock when a forklift driver, distracted by a phone call, almost hit him. The forklift's bumper grazed the worker’s shoulder, causing a small cut, but the employee managed to pull back before the vehicle could collide. The safety barrier that usually separates the walk lane from the forklift area was missing, which allowed the vehicle to get too close to the pedestrian path. The incident was quickly reported and the barrier was restored before the shift ended.

Day shift at Pipeline Yard D, a contractor was walking near the loading dock without his hard hat and safety glasses. He stepped onto a spill of lubricating oil and slipped, almost losing his footing. Luckily, he was only slightly off balance and no one else was affected. The incident shows that the contractor’s lack of PPE was a direct risk to his safety.

At Storage Site E on the night shift, a company employee was walking across the loading dock when a truck pulled out of the staging area without looking. The driver didn't see the person until he was about a meter away, and the employee had to dive out of the way just in time. The guard rail that normally separates the walk‑area from the vehicle lane was missing, which allowed the driver to get that close.

During the night shift at Storage Site E, a company employee was working on a maintenance task when the lockout/tagout switch on the gas compressor line failed to stay engaged. The employee noticed a slight pressure rise and immediately started shutting down the unit, but the valve slipped and released a small burst of high‑pressure gas that knocked him off his feet. Thankfully, he only sustained a minor burn and was taken to the first aid tent.

Day shift on Rig 4, a company employee was using the hydraulic jack to lift a heavy pipe segment. While the jack was operating, the safety guard that normally covers the moving arm fell off and was not replaced, leaving the operator exposed to a pinch point. The employee was able to stop the machine before the guard could hit them, but the incident highlighted a missing barrier that could have caused serious injury.

At Refinery B during the night shift, a contractor was attempting to enter a storage tank for inspection when he realized the entry hatch lock was jammed and could not be opened. He tried to force it and the lock cracked, causing a small crack in the hatch rim and a flash of sparks as the metal slipped. He pulled out quickly, but the cracked hatch left a gap that could have allowed fumes to escape, creating a potential inhalation hazard. The incident was stopped before anyone was injured.

Late night on the Pipeline Yard D, a contractor was tightening a coupler on a 16‑inch line when the pressure relief valve popped open, releasing a pungent gas cloud. He smelled the odor and immediately turned off the valve, but the fire suppression system hadn't been activated because the manual override panel was missing from that section of the yard. No one was hurt, but the contractor had to evacuate the area and the crew had to shut down the entire yard for a full leak check.

During the night shift at Storage Site E, a company employee was entering a vented silo to check a pressure gauge when the entry hatch latch failed to lock. The hatch fell open, exposing the worker to a sudden influx of hot vapor. He immediately backed out and called for an emergency release, but the incident highlighted the missing lock‑out tag on that hatch. The company is reviewing the hatch lock procedure.

During the night shift at Storage Site E, a company employee was attempting to close the isolation valve on the 120‑bar storage tank. The lock‑out tag was missing and the valve failed to fully shut, allowing a small burst of pressurized gas to escape. The employee smelled the gas and quickly moved to a safer distance, but the lack of proper isolation caused a brief, uncontrolled release that could have been much worse if the tank had been fully pressurized.

During the night shift on Rig 4, a company employee slipped on a wet patch near the feed inlet after a spill. He caught himself and avoided a fall, but the wet area was not marked and the spill containment barrier was missing. The employee warned the crew to clean up and put a spill kit in place.

During the night shift at Drilling Unit F, a company employee was working on the rig platform when a small piece of the safety rail slipped off the side. He nearly fell when he stepped over the gap, but was able to catch himself on a nearby pipe just before losing balance. The incident highlights the need to check the integrity of fall protection systems before starting work.

During the night shift on Rig 4, a contractor was moving a load of drilling mud without his hard hat or safety harness. The load slipped and slid toward the rig’s edge, but he caught it just in time. The incident highlighted how missing PPE can quickly turn a routine task into a serious risk.

At Drilling Unit F on the day shift, a company employee noticed a faint odor of gas while inspecting the blowout preventer line. The employee quickly shut the valve, but the pressure relief valve didn't actuate as expected, creating a small burst of flame that was immediately snuffed out with a portable fire extinguisher. No one was injured, but the incident exposed a missing seal on the valve flange that needs to be replaced before the next shift.

Late night at Pipeline Yard D, a contractor was walking across a wet patch left by a recent leak. The contractor slipped, twisted his ankle, and almost dropped a container of crude oil, but the container was secured and didn't spill. The spill pad was missing from that corner, so the hazard wasn't flagged until after the incident.

At Loading Bay G during the night shift, a company employee was working on the fuel transfer line when the lockout tag on the main power valve was not properly engaged. The valve accidentally opened, sending a burst of hot hydraulic fluid across the bay, but the employee was able to grab the emergency cut‑off switch in time and shut it off before anyone got burned. The incident highlighted a lapse in the energy isolation procedure and a missing safety barrier on the valve cover.

At the Maintenance Shop H on the day shift, a contractor was working on the feed line when he tried to start the pump without proper lock‑out. He reached for the isolation valve but it was stuck in the “open” position, so when he pulled it to close, it slipped back to open and the line sprang back. The contractor’s hand hit the sudden flow of gas and he had to quickly withdraw, but a small spray of high‑pressure gas hit his face. The incident was a near‑miss because the contractor didn’t sustain an injury, but the failure to lock out the energy source was a clear hazard.

During the night shift on Rig 4, a company employee was checking the isolation valves on the wellhead when the lock‑out tag slipped off, and the valve did not stay closed. The well started to flow a bit, so the employee had to quickly shut the valve manually, but the valve jammed and a small burst of pressure released into the pipe line, scalding a nearby hose line. No one was injured, but the incident shows the isolation procedure was not followed correctly and the safety barrier failed.

At Terminal C during the day shift, a company employee slipped on a wet patch left by a spill that wasn’t cleaned up. The floor was slick, but the employee caught themselves before falling and avoided injury, though they slipped again as they tried to recover. The incident highlighted a missed cleanup and the need for better signage around the spill area.

At Refinery B on the night shift, a contractor was working on the valve maintenance rig when the guard on the hydraulic press fell off. He almost got his hand caught in the opening, but a quick reaction stopped it. The guard was missing its lock‑in, so the equipment could have caused a serious injury.

At Terminal C during the day shift, a company employee entered a venting tank that was still in a partial‑fill state. The ventilation system was off, so the air had no fresh supply and the worker felt a sudden, faint tingling in his chest when the pressure dropped. He immediately pulled out, used a portable oxygen tank, and exited the tank with no injuries, but the incident shows the ventilation lockout/tag‑out procedure was not followed.

During the night shift at Terminal C, a company employee noticed a faint hissing sound near the storage tanks. The smell of gasoline grew stronger, and a small spark was seen from the leaking pipe, but the fire suppression system kicked in before anything ignited. The employee quickly sealed the pipe with a temporary clamp, and the incident was logged as a near‑miss.

On the day shift at Rig 4, a contractor was climbing the ladder to replace a valve when he slipped on a wet rung and almost fell to the rig floor. He caught himself with a nearby handrail, but the handrail was only half the height it should be, so he barely avoided a serious fall. The incident shows that the ladder safety guard was not properly installed.

During the night shift at Refinery B, a company employee entered a venting line that had not been properly sealed. The ventilation fan was still on, so when the worker pulled the cover off, a burst of hot air rushed in and the employee was knocked over, breaking a wrench on his hand. The incident was quickly stopped but the employee had to get medical attention for a sprained wrist.

During the night shift at Drilling Unit F, a company employee was seen walking through the rig bay without a hard hat and safety harness. The worker was moving a hydraulic jack near the main wellhead, and the lack of PPE could have led to a serious head injury if a falling object had hit them. The incident was reported immediately, and the employee was reminded to wear the required gear before continuing work.

During the day shift in Pipeline Yard D, a company employee slipped on a slick patch near the scaffold edge while moving a pallet. He nearly fell over the 15‑foot guardrail, but the railing held, and he was able to regain footing. No injuries, but the incident highlights the risk of footing near elevated platforms.

Night shift at Terminal C, a company employee was checking the storage tanks when a small flame flickered under the metal cover of a gas line. The employee immediately shut the valve and called for a gas detector sweep, but the fire barrier that should have covered the opening was missing, so the flame spread a bit before the fire extinguisher was used. No one was injured and the leak was contained, but the incident shows the barrier was not in place.

During the day shift at Refinery B, a contractor was performing maintenance on the 200‑bar pressure vessel when the isolation valve failed to lock open. The valve slipped back into the closed position, and the contractor was suddenly exposed to the pressurized line. He managed to grab the valve handle in time, but the incident highlighted a clear failure in the energy isolation procedure and the lack of a secondary lockout tag.

Night shift at Storage Site E, a company employee was walking across the loading dock when a small pallet of cracked crates slipped from an unsecured stack and rolled onto the floor. The employee brushed past it without tripping, but it was a close call that highlighted the lack of proper pallet securing and spill containment in that area.

During the night shift at Refinery B, a contractor was trying to enter a maintenance pit for a valve replacement. He was using the ladder provided, but the ladder was already down and a temporary guard rail had been removed for a different job. While climbing, the contractor slipped and nearly fell into the pit, but was caught by a safety net that was still in place. The incident was stopped before any serious injury occurred, but the guard rail should have been restored immediately.

During the day shift at Refinery B, a company employee was walking through the piping corridor without a hard hat. A section of the pipe was leaking a small amount of hot vapor, and the employee's bare head would have taken a severe burn if the leak had become larger, but the leak stopped quickly and he was able to step aside in time. The incident shows that the employee was not wearing the required PPE, which could have caused a serious injury if the leak had worsened.

During the day shift in Pipeline Yard D, a contractor was welding on the east section of the pipe line. He was not wearing the required hard hat or the safety glasses that the yard’s PPE checklist mandates. When he struck the metal pipe, the heat caused a small splatter, and a piece of hot metal landed on his bare arm. The worker quickly pulled his arm back, and the fire was doused by the nearby water spray. No injuries were reported, but the incident highlighted a clear lapse in PPE compliance.

Night shift at Refinery B: I was walking along the loading dock when a service truck rolled into the pedestrian zone because the speed limiter was off and the barrier gate was jammed. The driver nearly hit me, but I was able to step aside in time. The incident shows a clear gap in vehicle-pedestrian safety, and the barrier failure needs immediate inspection.

During the night shift at Storage Site E, a company employee slipped on a wet patch of oil left from a recent leak. The employee nearly fell into a shallow pit that had no barrier around it. The fall could have caused a serious injury, but the employee only got up and walked away without any damage.

During the night shift at Pipeline Yard D, a company employee was walking across a spill containment area that had been marked only with a small chalk line. He was not wearing his required high‑visibility vest or safety boots. The employee slipped on a slick patch of crude oil, nearly falling into the spill, and his left glove came off, exposing his hand to the chemical. The incident was reported as a near‑miss and prompted an immediate stop‑work order for that section of the yard.

At Rig 4 on the day shift a contractor was tightening the clamp on the high‑pressure line, but the isolation valve was stuck open. When he released the line, a burst of pressure pushed the pipe’s support out of place, causing a small splatter of hydraulic fluid onto the floor. The contractor grabbed a wet rag and moved away, but the spill could have ignited if a spark had been present. The incident was reported immediately, and the valve was inspected for mechanical failure.

During the day shift at Terminal C, a contractor was welding on the outer wall of the storage tank. He didn't wear his safety goggles or hearing protection, and his workbench was set up too close to the spill containment barrier. The welding sparks landed on the barrier, creating a small fire that was quickly doused, but the contractor’s lack of PPE left him exposed to heat and fumes.

During the day shift at Refinery B, a company employee was working on the top of the storage tank stack when the handrail she was holding slipped. She almost fell to the platform below, but the fall was caught by a nearby safety net that was already in place. The net was damaged from the impact, so she had to wait for a replacement before continuing her work.

At Rig 4 during the day shift a company employee slipped on a wet patch of floor left after the last cleaning. The spill was right next to the pipe support area and there was no signage warning of the slick. The worker stumbled, caught on the edge of a metal guardrail, and almost lost balance, but was able to regain footing without injury.

At Storage Site E during the day shift, a contractor was moving a pallet of solvent drums when a faulty pipe started leaking a light, flammable gas. The contractor noticed the odor and immediately moved to a safe spot, but the hose was not secured, so a small flame from a nearby welding torch sparked a brief puff that was quickly extinguished by a fire extinguisher. The contractor reported the incident, and the area was isolated while the leak was fixed and the hose replaced.

During the night shift at Storage Site E, a company employee slipped on a slick patch of oil that had leaked from a cracked pipe near the loading bay. The employee caught themselves before falling, but the spill was spreading over a marked walk‑way, creating a trip hazard for others. The spill was quickly isolated and cleaned up, and a temporary flag was placed to warn the crew.

Night shift at Refinery B: A company employee was entering a storage tank through a manhole. The air‑quality monitor detected a drop in oxygen levels to 17% as he descended, but the alarm didn’t trigger because the sensor was not properly connected. The worker had to stop, don a self‑contained breathing apparatus, and recheck the readings before continuing.

At Rig 4 during the night shift, a company employee entered the casing head hatch without the required air‑monitoring checks. The hatch seal had been loose for weeks and was not replaced, so a small amount of stale air rushed in when the employee opened it. He felt a sudden pressure change but managed to exit safely before any gas reached dangerous levels. The incident highlighted the missing safety barrier and the need for immediate seal replacement.

During the night shift at Terminal C, a company employee was walking toward the loading dock when a forklift suddenly accelerated out of its bay and collided with the pedestrian walkway. The employee was knocked over, suffered a minor shoulder injury, and had to be assisted off the floor. The incident highlighted that the safety barrier between the forklift storage area and the pedestrian path was either missing or had been removed for maintenance, creating a clear vehicle-pedestrian interaction hazard.

During the day shift at Storage Site E, a contractor was working near the loading bay without wearing the required high‑visibility vest and safety boots. He slipped on a wet patch and almost fell onto the conveyor belt, but was stopped by the guard rail. The incident highlighted the contractor's PPE noncompliance and the need for stricter enforcement before work begins.

During the day shift at Refinery B, a company employee was walking down the service lane when a maintenance truck, moving slowly, swerved to avoid a fallen pipe. The employee had to duck to avoid the wheel, and the truck’s side mirror hit the guard rail, sending a small pile of gravel into the pedestrian zone. Luckily, no one was injured, but the incident highlighted that the barrier was not tall enough for vehicle impact.

During the night shift at Pipeline Yard D a contractor was working on a segment of the main line when the isolation valve failed to close properly. The pressure relief system kicked in, but a burst pipe caused a spray of hot oil that almost hit the worker’s jacket. Luckily the contractor was wearing the proper PPE and stepped out of the way, but the incident shows the isolation system didn’t lock out as it should have.

At Loading Bay G on the night shift, a company employee slipped on a puddle of water that had leaked from a damaged pipe. The employee didn’t fall, but he almost lost his footing while reaching for a crate. The spill was immediately cleaned up and a warning sign was put up to prevent future slips.

During the day shift at Terminal C, a company employee was working on the tank farm when the isolation valve on the 12‑bar line failed to lock. The valve opened slightly, sending a burst of high‑pressure gas that knocked the worker to the floor. He was able to recover and the gas was vented, but the incident shows a clear isolation failure that could have caused a serious release.

During the day shift at Rig 4, a company employee entered a small venting shaft to replace a faulty seal. The employee didn’t secure the proper breathing apparatus, and when the shaft was opened the pressure dropped quickly, causing a sudden rush of cold air that knocked him off balance. He caught himself on the ladder, but the sudden airflow had forced a loose pipe segment to shift, exposing exposed wiring. The incident was a near-miss; the employee was not injured, but the shaft lacked a proper safety barrier, which made the situation hazardous.

Night shift at Refinery B, a company employee tripped over a loose pipe clamp that had fallen on the conveyor belt line. He nearly fell into the machinery, but caught himself on a nearby support bracket and avoided injury. The clamp had not been resecured after maintenance, creating a slip/trip hazard that could have caused a serious incident.

Night shift at Refinery B: a contractor was hanging on a ladder to replace a filter on the 8‑foot high vent stack. He lost his footing, slipped and nearly fell. The fall was stopped by the guardrail that was still in place, but the ladder was damaged and a piece of the rung broke off, leaving a gap that could have let someone else fall if they'd been below.

On the night shift at Rig 4, a company employee slipped on a wet spot near the haul truck loading area. The spill had been left uncovered after a minor leak from a valve line, and there was no wet‑surface warning sign in place. The employee only lost balance and stumbled, but the fall could have been serious if the hydraulic pump were running.

During the day shift at Rig 4, a company employee was seen walking through the hot‑work area without a face shield. He had been wearing his standard jacket and gloves, but the visor had been removed because it was deemed inconvenient. The lack of eye protection exposed him to a spray of molten metal that splashed onto his face, causing a minor burn and forcing him to stop work for medical treatment.

At Maintenance Shop H on the night shift, a company employee was working on a hydraulic press when the safety interlock on the machine failed to engage. The operator was forced to stop the press manually, but the emergency stop button was not within reach, so the machine continued running for a few seconds before the operator pulled the fire alarm. He narrowly avoided a serious injury when the moving part almost caught his hand.

During the day shift on Rig 4, a contractor was seen walking across the work area without wearing a hard hat or high‑visibility vest. He stepped over a temporary safety barrier that was already in place for the day, but the barrier was not secured and collapsed onto his foot, causing a small cut. The incident was reported immediately, and the contractor received a safety briefing before resuming work.
